meta.title: Ethiopian Liturgical Calendar Engine
meta.subtitle: Documentation
meta.description: A validation and research environment for the Ethiopian liturgical calendar engine being developed for a Christian worship mobile app targeting Ethiopian Lutheran congregations.

sections.heading: Overview
sections.body:
This tool is a validation and research environment for the Ethiopian liturgical calendar engine being developed for a Christian worship mobile app targeting Ethiopian Lutheran (Mekane Yesus) congregations. The engine must correctly compute the Ethiopian church year — movable feasts, fasting periods, seasons, and the four-year Evangelist cycle — entirely offline, using the Ethiopian calendar as the native date system.

This documentation explains the problem we are solving, what we analyzed, how the algorithm works, and how we intend to integrate it into the final application.

sections.heading: The Problem
sections.intro:
Most Ethiopian calendar tools solve the civil calendar problem — converting Gregorian dates to Ethiopian dates, displaying the 13-month structure, handling Pagume. That is the easy layer.

The worship app requires something deeper: a liturgical calendar engine. This means knowing not just what day it is in the Ethiopian calendar, but what the church year says about that day — which season it is, whether it is a fasting day, which feast is being observed, and which gospel year the church is in.

The specific challenges we identified:

items.heading: The new year mismatch
items.body: The Ethiopian civil year begins on Meskerem 1 (September 11 or 12). The Lutheran church year begins at Advent, which falls in late November or December. These two year starts do not align, and no existing Mekane Yesus app has cleanly solved this. Several published apps skip seasons or cut content at the year boundary because they tried to force one year structure onto the other.

items.heading: The denomination gap
items.body: The Ethiopian Orthodox Tewahedo Church (EOTC) has a well-documented calendrical system. The Mekane Yesus church follows the same Ethiopian calendar for feast dates and fasting periods but has its own lectionary — its own assigned readings, sermon themes, and commemorations. No clean public dataset exists for this layer. It must be sourced directly from the Ethiopian Evangelical Church Mekane Yesus (EECMY).

items.heading: The four-year Evangelist cycle
items.body: The Ethiopian church year is organized into a repeating four-year cycle, each year named after one of the four Evangelists — John, Matthew, Mark, and Luke. Each Evangelist year carries its own gospel readings and sermon themes. Any correct lectionary implementation must know which Evangelist year it is computing for.

items.heading: Offline-first requirement
items.body: The app must work without internet access, which is a real constraint for Ethiopian users. This means all calendar computation and all liturgical data must be precomputed and bundled in the app. No live API calls.

subsections.heading: Three open source repositories
subsections.intro: We analyzed three existing Ethiopian calendar implementations:

items.name: Kenat
items.description: The most complete modern implementation. Contains a full Bahire Hasab engine, Gregorian-to-Ethiopian and Ethiopian-to-Gregorian conversion, all movable Christian feasts, fasting periods with start and end dates, Islamic holiday computation, and full Amharic and English localization. Well tested. This is the primary source for our engine.

items.name: AbushakirJs
items.description: An older class-based implementation of the same algorithm. Uses the same tewsak offset table. Useful as a cross-reference to validate the math.

items.name: Ethiocal
items.description: The same Bahire Hasab algorithm implemented in Go. Used only as an independent verification of the intermediate computation values.

subsections.heading: What Bahire Hasab actually is
subsections.body:
Bahire Hasab — literally "the calculation of the sea" in Ge'ez — is the traditional Ethiopian method for computing the church year. It derives from the Alexandrian computus, the same mathematical tradition that the Coptic Church uses, which in turn traces back to the calculations of Anatolius of Laodicea in the third century.

The system computes a single anchor point each year — the Fast of Nineveh — and then derives every other movable feast as a fixed offset from that anchor. This is elegant: once you know Nineveh, you know Easter, Ascension, Pentecost, and all fasting periods.

steps.heading: Establish the cosmic year
steps.explanation: Amete Alem means "year of the world" in Ge'ez. The Ethiopian Orthodox Church counts years from the date of creation, which by their reckoning was 5500 years before the Incarnation. Adding 5500 to the Ethiopian year gives the cosmic year count. This number drives everything else.

steps.heading: Compute the lunar constants
steps.code:
medeb   = ameteAlem % 19
wenber  = medeb === 0 ? 18 : medeb - 1
abektie = (wenber × 11) % 30
metqi   = (wenber × 19) % 30
steps.explanation: The number 19 here is the Metonic cycle — the period after which lunar phases repeat on the same calendar dates. Every 19 years the moon returns to the same position relative to the solar year. This is the same cycle used in the Western computus for Easter calculation. Medeb is the position in the 19-year cycle. Wenber is the adjusted lunar base. Abektie and Metqi are intermediate lunar values used to find the full moon that anchors the fast.

steps.heading: Find the Beale Metqi (full moon day)
steps.code:
bealeMetqiMonth = metqi > 14 ? Tir (month 5) : Yekatit (month 6)
bealeMetqiDay   = metqi
steps.explanation: The Beale Metqi is the liturgical full moon — the ecclesiastical new moon date that anchors the fast cycle. Depending on whether metqi falls above or below 14, the full moon lands in either Tir or Yekatit.

steps.heading: Find the day of the week and apply the tewsak
steps.explanation: The Beale Metqi day of the week is computed. The tewsak ("addition" in Ge'ez) is the number of days to add to reach the next Monday, which is where Nineveh begins. Each weekday has a fixed tewsak value.

steps.heading: Derive the Fast of Nineveh
steps.body: The Fast of Nineveh is the anchor. Its date is mebajaHamer in either Tir or Yekatit, adjusted for month overflow. From this single date, every other feast and fast in the Ethiopian church year is computed by adding a fixed number of days.

tewsakTable.heading: Movable feast offsets from Nineveh
tewsakTable.note: Easter is offset +69 from the Fast of Nineveh. This is the Alexandrian computus expressed in Ethiopian calendar arithmetic.

sections.heading: Fixed Feasts and Fasting Periods
sections.intro: In addition to the movable feasts, the Ethiopian church year has fixed observances keyed by Ethiopian calendar date:

sections.heading: The Four-Year Evangelist Cycle
sections.body: The Ethiopian Orthodox and Mekane Yesus churches organize the liturgical year into a repeating four-year cycle. Each year is named after one of the four Evangelists and is associated with a particular gospel as the primary gospel for that year's readings.
implications: Sermon themes, gospel readings, and some commemorations change depending on which Evangelist year it is.
Any correct implementation of the Mekane Yesus lectionary must track the Evangelist year and serve the appropriate content.
The four-year cycle also means that Easter shifts considerably across a four-year window. In some years Fasika falls in Miazia (April range), in others in Megabit (March range).
This affects how many Sundays fall in certain seasons and how the entire movable feast arc is distributed across the civil year.
The Four Years view in this tool exists specifically to visualize this variation.

sections.heading: How We Intend to Solve It

subsections.heading: Architecture decision
subsections.body:
The app will run the liturgical engine entirely in the Ethiopian calendar. Ethiopian dates are the native coordinate system. Gregorian dates are only used for conversion at the display layer or for cross-referencing with the LSB lectionary data.

The engine is structured in three layers:

layers.name: Civil calendar
layers.description: Gregorian↔Ethiopian conversion, 13-month structure, leap year handling, Pagume. Sourced from Kenat.

layers.name: Liturgical rules engine
layers.description: Bahire Hasab computation, movable feast resolution, fasting period assignment, fixed feast lookup, Evangelist year classification. Built in this project.

layers.name: Denominational content
layers.description: Mekane Yesus lectionary readings, sermon themes, Sunday propers, commemorations. This layer is pending. We are in the process of obtaining the official dataset from EECMY. Once received, it will be encoded as a structured JSON dataset keyed by Evangelist year and week number, then merged with the engine output at query time.

subsections.heading: Precomputed dataset
subsections.body: For the offline-first mobile app, the engine output for Ethiopian years 2010–2030 will be precomputed and bundled as a static JSON file. This covers all feast dates, fasting periods, and Evangelist year assignments for the range 2017–2038 in the Gregorian calendar — more than sufficient for the initial release. The computation will be re-run and the bundle updated as needed for future years.

subsections.heading: Validation process
subsections.body: Before integrating into the app, every computed feast date is being cross-checked against:
sources: The Kenat test suite (which contains verified dates)
The AbushakirJs test suite as an independent verification
Manual spot checks against known Fasika dates for recent years
subsections.closing: This tool is the validation environment for that process.

sections.heading: Contact
sections.body: This project is being developed by Lukas Brocker and Cherinet, working independently as open source collaborators. If you have access to Mekane Yesus liturgical data, EECMY calendar publications, or EOTC sanctoral calendar materials and are willing to contribute, we would like to hear from you.
lookingFor: The official EECMY four-year lectionary tables (readings by Evangelist year and week)
Mekane Yesus Sunday sermon theme assignments
EOTC sanctoral calendar data (saints days keyed by Ethiopian date)
Any published Mekane Yesus worship resource in digital form
